transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. It's, uh, nice to meet you too. Well, honestly, I'm here because... I just haven't been feeling right in my head lately. I work as a personal care aide, you know, helping folks in their homes, and it's a job that really requires you to be on the ball. You have to track a lot of different things at once. But lately, my head just feels incredibly foggy. It's like I'm trying to think through a thick bowl of soup or something. 

And because of that, I'm starting to make all these little mistakes in my client notes. We have to keep these really detailed daily logs for the agencies and the families—what they ate, their vitals, all that—and I'm usually so meticulous about it. I took some college classes back in the day, so I know how to document things properly. But now I'm writing down the wrong times or missing checkboxes. Or, even worse, I'll stand up to go do something for a client, walk into the kitchen, and just completely forget what I was about to do. I'll just stand there staring at the counter, totally blank. 

It’s really frustrating because that just isn’t like me at all. I pride myself on being sharp and reliable for my clients, and this whole foggy feeling is just really throwing me off my game. I figured I needed to come in and talk to someone about it before I end up making a bigger mistake at work, you know? It's just really bothering me how much I'm struggling to just keep my thoughts straight.
Beyond this brain fog, have you been feeling sad, down, or have you lost interest in the things you usually enjoy?

Yeah, actually... it's kind of hard to explain, but I'll try. Lately, I've been waking up, and before my alarm even finishes going off, before I even sit up or put my feet on the floor, I just have this... this incredibly heavy, empty feeling right in the middle of my chest. It's almost like a physical weight just sitting there. 

And I'll just lie there for a minute, looking at the ceiling, trying to figure out why I feel so down. I mean, I still get up and do what I need to do. I have to, right? People are depending on me. So I get up, I get dressed, I drive over to my clients' houses... and I can get through my shift. I can put on a smile, I can talk to people, I can chat with the families about the weather or whatever's on the news or what they had for dinner. I'm sure to them, I look like the exact same guy I've always been. 

But inside? Inside, I'm just... I'm just sad. It's this deep, flat sadness that doesn't really go away. It's exhausting, honestly, having to pretend everything is normal when you feel that hollow on the inside. I can be right in the middle of a conversation, smiling and nodding while I'm helping someone with their physical therapy exercises or whatever, but internally I just feel completely flat and empty. It really takes it out of you, having to bridge that gap between how you look and how you actually feel all day long, just carrying that heaviness around in your chest from the minute you wake up until you finally go back to sleep.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let me think back... it's been a little while now. I'd say this whole low, heavy feeling, along with that awful brain fog I mentioned earlier, has been hanging over me for about a month. Maybe exactly a month, actually. I remember it started right around the time I was assigned to this new client—Mr. Henderson, a really nice older gentleman who needs help with his mobility after a hip replacement. I was so excited to take on his case because his daughter was just so sweet and really needed the support, but right from my first week with them, I started feeling this... this shift, you know? 

At first, I thought maybe I was just tired from adjusting to the new schedule, or maybe coming down with a cold, because you know how you get that achy, heavy feeling when you're fighting something off. But the cold never came, and the feeling just stayed. And then the guilt started creeping in, too. I'd be sitting there with Mr. Henderson, watching him struggle to do his leg lifts, and I'd just feel so incredibly guilty that I couldn't be more present, more upbeat for him. Like, here he is, working so hard to walk again, and I can barely muster the energy to care about my own life. 

So yeah, it's been about four solid weeks of waking up with that weight on my chest, trying to push through the fog, and feeling guilty that I'm not doing a better job for the people who rely on me. It feels like a lot longer, to be honest, because every single day just drags on when you feel like this, but if I look at the calendar, it's definitely been right around a month since this whole cloud settled over me.
Have these symptoms been severe enough that you have had to take time off work or call out of your shifts recently?

Well, no, I haven't actually called out or taken time off. I've managed to keep showing up, you know? Like I said, people are depending on me, and I can't just leave them hanging. But... it hasn't been easy, and I definitely wouldn't say I'm functioning at a hundred percent. 

Because of that brain fog I was talking about earlier, the whole struggling to keep things straight... I've actually had to start asking my coworkers to double-check my client documentation before I submit it. Which is so embarrassing, honestly. I mean, I'm a grown man, I've been doing this job for a while, and I'm usually the one helping the new hires figure out the charting system. But now, I'll fill out Mr. Henderson's daily log, or Mrs. Gable's medication chart, and I'll just have this nagging, awful feeling that I've messed something up. So I'll pull aside Sarah or Dave—they're a couple of the other aides I work closely with—and I'll be like, "Hey, can you just glance over this? Make sure I didn't write down that I gave him his meds at 8 PM instead of 8 AM?" And they're nice about it, they really are, but I hate having to ask. It just makes me feel so incompetent, like I can't even trust my own brain to do the basic parts of my job anymore.

And it's not just at work, either. It's bleeding into things at home, too. My wife, bless her heart, she's had to take over a lot of the stuff I usually handle. I'm usually the one who pays the bills, keeps track of the budget, schedules the appointments for the kids... I've always been good with numbers and details, probably because of those college classes I took. But lately, I just... I can't. I'll sit down at the computer to pay the electric bill, and I'll just stare at the screen, totally blank, just like when I walk into the kitchen at work. I missed a credit card payment a couple of weeks ago because I just completely forgot what day it was, which has literally never happened before. 

So my wife finally just said, "Look, let me handle the bills and the calendar for a while." And I know she's just trying to help, and I appreciate it, I really do, but it just adds to that whole guilty, heavy feeling I carry around all day. It's like I'm letting everyone down—my clients, my coworkers, my wife... I'm just not as reliable with the details right now, and it's incredibly frustrating to watch myself slip up on things that used to be second nature to me. So no, I haven't taken time off, but I'm definitely not operating normally, that's for sure.
Looking back further than just this past month, have you ever felt this way before, or is this the first time in your life you've experienced this kind of persistent heaviness and mental fog?

Well, no, honestly... I really don't think I have. I mean, I've been racking my brain trying to think of a time, just to give myself some hope, you know? Like, 'oh, I got through this before, I can get through it again.' But... no. I mean, sure, everybody has bad days, or even bad weeks. Like when my dad passed away a few years ago, obviously I was grieving and very sad then, or back when the kids were toddlers and my wife and I were just surviving on coffee and two hours of sleep... you feel exhausted and overwhelmed then, sure. 

But this? This specific kind of... of heavy, empty, foggy thing that just won't lift? No, never. I was actually just telling my wife the other night—we were sitting in the living room, she was looking over the budget since she took that over, and she asked me pretty much the exact same question you just did. She said, 'Honey, have you ever felt like this before?' And I just had to look at her and say no. Because I've always been the guy who bounces back. I've always been the steady one, the rock. Even back when I was taking those college classes in my twenties, working part-time and studying for exams, I'd get stressed, but I'd just push through and shake it off. I've had tough clients at work before, too, people who really test your patience, but I'd just leave it at the door when I clocked out.

So to have this feeling just... stick to me, like wet sand, for a solid month? It's completely uncharted territory for me. I've never had a time where my brain just wouldn't cooperate like this, where I couldn't just snap myself out of a funk by going for a drive or watching a good football game. It's actually really unsettling, to be forty-three years old and suddenly feel like you're completely foreign to yourself, like your own mind is just refusing to do the things it's always done. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like the old me again, but it just hasn't happened. So yeah, I'm pretty confident this is the very first time I've ever dealt with anything even remotely like this.
